titleStmt.title: The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information
titleStmt.author: George A. Miller

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The recurring limit of about seven in absolute judgment, attention and immediate memory, and whether those limits are one thing or several.
span.quote: My problem is that I have been persecuted by an integer.

span.label: existence
span.quote: There is a clear and definite limit to the accuracy with which we can identify absolutely the magnitude of a unidimensional stimulus variable.

span.label: span of absolute judgment and span of immediate memory
span.quote: First, the span of absolute judgment and the span of immediate memory impose severe limitations on the amount of information that we are able to receive, process, and remember.

span.label: review
span.quote: I shall begin my case history by telling you about some experiments that tested how accurately people can assign numbers to the magnitudes of various aspects of a stimulus.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the human observer behaves like a limited-capacity communication channel: absolute judgment saturates at a channel capacity of about 2.5 bits (~7 categories)
span.quote: This asymptotic value we take to be the channel capacity of the observer

span.label: Treating the observer as a communication channel makes the limit measurable: input information is raised until transmitted information stops rising, and that asymptote is the capacity
span.quote: This asymptotic value we take to be the channel capacity of the observer: it represents the greatest amount of information that he can give us about the stimulus on the basis of an absolute judgment.

span.label: Immediate memory holds a fixed number of chunks rather than a fixed number of bits, which is why it behaves unlike absolute judgment
span.quote: The span of immediate memory seems to be almost independent of the number of bits per chunk, at least over the range that has been examined to date.

span.label: Because the limit is in chunks, packing more information into each chunk raises how much can be held without raising the count
span.quote: Since the memory span is a fixed number of chunks, we can increase the number of bits of information that it contains simply by building larger and larger chunks, each chunk containing more information than before.

span.label: Recoding is the operation that builds bigger chunks: group the input, name the group, remember the name
span.quote: There are many ways to do this recoding, but probably the simplest is to group the input events, apply a new name to the group, and then remember the new name rather than the original input events.

span.label: Adding dimensions and accepting cruder judgments on each raises the span of absolute judgment far beyond seven
span.quote: 91] more dimensions and requiring crude, binary, yes-no judgments on each attribute we can extend the span of absolute judgment from seven to at least 150.

span.label: the recurrence of 'seven' across channel capacity and memory span may be merely coincidental
span.quote: And yet when we examine the matter more closely, there seems to be a reasonable suspicion that it is nothing more than a coincidence.

span.label: The suggested span of perceptual dimensionality (about ten) is stated to have no supporting objective evidence.
span.quote: I suspect that there is also a span of perceptual dimensionality and that this span is somewhere in the neighborhood of ten, but I must add at once that there is no objective evidence to support this suspicion.

span.label: Some reported channel-capacity values are probably underestimates because data were pooled across subjects before computing transmitted information.
span.quote: I should add, however, that these values are apt to be slightly too low because the data from all subjects were pooled before the transmitted information was computed.

span.label: The central theoretical unit, the chunk, is not precisely defined.
span.quote: The contrast of the terms bit and chunk also serves to highlight the fact that we are not very definite about what constitutes a chunk of information.

span.label: The subitizing comparison rests on a guess, since the number-estimation data were never analysed in informational terms.
span.quote: The data on number estimates have not been analyzed in informational terms; but on the basis of the published data I would guess that the subjects transmitted something more than four bits of information about the number of dots.

span.label: The paper's own closing position is that the recurring seven is probably coincidence, not one underlying limit
span.quote: Perhaps there is something deep and profound behind all these sevens, something just calling out for us to discover it. But I suspect that it is only a pernicious, Pythagorean coincidence.

span.label: The unit that the memory limit is counted in is admitted to be undefined
span.quote: The contrast of the terms bit and chunk also serves to highlight the fact that we are not very definite about what constitutes a chunk of information.

span.label: The chunk independence holds only over the range tested so far, which the author states rather than assumes
span.quote: The span of immediate memory seems to be almost independent of the number of bits per chunk, at least over the range that has been examined to date.

span.label: The span of seven is claimed for unidimensional judgments specifically, not judgments in general
span.quote: I would propose to call this limit the span of absolute judgment , and I maintain that for unidimensional judgments this span is usually somewhere in the neighborhood of seven.

span.label: The information-theoretic machinery is deliberately paraphrased away, so the argument as presented cannot be checked against the formalism it rests on
span.quote: In the interests of communication I have suppressed the technical details of information measurement and have tried to express the ideas in more familiar terms; I hope this paraphrase will not lead you to think they are not useful in research.

span.label: analyzing the limits of human perception and memory using information theory (channel capacity, bits)
span.quote: the results are analyzed in terms of the concepts of information theory

span.label: Shannon's information measure, the channel and its capacity, carried into psychology - and the paper is explicit that the experiments would not exist without it
span.quote: Since these experiments would not have been done without the appearance of information theory on the psychological scene, and since the results are analyzed in terms of the concepts of information theory, I shall have to preface my discussion with a few remarks about this theory.

span.label: A translation table offered in the other direction, so psychologists could read the information measure as the variance they already knew
span.quote: The "amount of information" is exactly the same concept that we have talked about for years under the name of "variance."

span.label: span of immediate memory
span.quote: Since there is a large discrepancy in the amount of information recalled in these two cases, we suspect at once that a recoding procedure could be used to increase the span of immediate memory for binary digits.

span.label: recoding
span.quote: Since there is a large discrepancy in the amount of information recalled in these two cases, we suspect at once that a recoding procedure could be used to increase the span of immediate memory for binary digits.

span.label: seven - the span of absolute judgment: about seven categories distinguishable along one dimension, a limit in BITS
span.quote: I would propose to call this limit the span of absolute judgment , and I maintain that for unidimensional judgments this span is usually somewhere in the neighborhood of seven.

span.label: seven - the span of immediate memory: about seven items retained, a limit in CHUNKS and almost independent of the bits in each
span.quote: Everybody knows that there is a finite span of immediate memory and that for a lot of different kinds of test materials this span is about seven items in length.

span.label: seven - the span of attention: about six objects taken in at a glance, a third limit with a similar number and a different mechanism
span.quote: I have just shown you that there is a span of absolute judgment that can distinguish about seven categories and that there is a span of attention that will encompass about six objects at a glance.

span.label: amount of information - as the paper translates it for the reader: variance, in the ordinary statistical sense
span.quote: The "amount of information" is exactly the same concept that we have talked about for years under the name of "variance."

span.label: amount of TRANSMITTED information - covariance or correlation between input and output, a different quantity that shares most of its name
span.quote: There are two simple rules to follow. Whenever I refer to "amount of information," you will understand "variance." And whenever I refer to "amount of transmitted information," you will understand "covariance" or "correlation."

span.label: builds-on → information theory (channel capacity)
span.quote: This asymptotic value we take to be the channel capacity of the observer: it represents the greatest amount of information that he can give us about the stimulus on the basis of an absolute judgment.

span.label: replicates → Hayes (10), memory-span experiment with five kinds of test material
span.quote: There is nothing wrong with Hayes's experiment, because Pollack ( 16 ) repeated it much more elaborately and got essentially the same result.

span.label: replicates → Hake and Garner (8), absolute judgment of visual position
span.quote: The Hake-Garner experiment has been repeated by Coonan and Klemmer.

span.label: builds-on → Külpe (14), abstraction experiment
span.quote: These multidimensional judgments are strongly reminiscent of the abstraction experiment of Külpe ( 14 ).

span.label: extends → information theory as imported into psychology
span.quote: Informational concepts have already proved valuable in the study of discrimination and of language; they promise a great deal in the study of learning and memory; and it has even been proposed that they can be useful in the study of concept formation.

span.label: critiques → the assumption that immediate memory is limited by the same quantity as absolute judgment
span.quote: If the amount of information in the span of immediate memory is a constant, then the span should be short when the individual items contain a lot of information and the span should be long when the items contain little information.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · span of absolute judgment —distinct-from→ span of immediate memory
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span named only `span of immediate memory`, in a conditional ('If immediate memory is like absolute judgment...'). This sentence names BOTH and states the distinction outright - and states it against the coincidence that would hide it, which is the whole point of the edge.
span.quote: If immediate memory is like absolute judgment, then it should follow that the invariant feature in the span of immediate memory is also the amount of information that an observer can retain.

span.label: span of attention —distinct-from→ span of absolute judgment
span.quote: I have just shown you that there is a span of absolute judgment that can distinguish about seven categories and that there is a span of attention that will encompass about six objects at a glance.

span.label: span of absolute judgment —operationalised-as→ channel capacity
span.quote: This asymptotic value we take to be the channel capacity of the observer: it represents the greatest amount of information that he can give us about the stimulus on the basis of an absolute judgment.

span.label: chunk —distinct-from→ bit
span.quote: The contrast of the terms bit and chunk also serves to highlight the fact that we are not very definite about what constitutes a chunk of information.

span.label: span of immediate memory —operationalised-as→ chunk
span.quote: Since the memory span is a fixed number of chunks, we can increase the number of bits of information that it contains simply by building larger and larger chunks, each chunk containing more information than before.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · recoding —causes→ chunk
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span describes WHAT recoding IS - 'There are many ways to do this recoding, but probably the simplest is to group the input events, apply a new name to the group, and then remember the new name rather than the original input' - and names only one endpoint. It carries NO EFFECT CUE AT ALL, so a `causes` edge standing on it would fail the gate's own causes test today; it predates that rule. The replacement names both endpoints and states the effect: 'this kind of recoding INCREASES the bits per chunk'. Both spans are Miller's and both are accurate; the second is evidence for THIS TYPE and the first is not. Selected from TOOLS/find_regrounding_candidates.py after reading six offers and DECLINING FIVE - cook2013's candidate carried a glued sentence-case heading, schmidhuber2015's was a contents listing, and grilli2016's and miller1956[4]'s existing spans were STRONGER for their types than the offers ('a modular structure is a particular block structure'; 'the memory span is a fixed number of chunks'). A both-endpoint span is not an improvement if it is weaker evidence for the type.
span.quote: There are many ways to do this recoding, but probably the simplest is to group the input events, apply a new name to the group, and then remember the new name rather than the original input events.

span.label: transmitted information —same-as→ variance
span.quote: There are two simple rules to follow. Whenever I refer to "amount of information," you will understand "variance." And whenever I refer to "amount of transmitted information," you will understand "covariance" or "correlation."

span.label: communication channel —operationalised-as→ absolute judgment
span.quote: In the experiments on absolute judgment, the observer is considered to be a communication channel.

span.label: noise —contrasted-with→ transmitted information
span.quote: If we measure this correlation, then we can say how much of the output variance is attributable to the input and how much is due to random fluctuations or "noise" introduced by the system during transmission.

span.label: information theory —causes→ absolute judgment
span.quote: Since these experiments would not have been done without the appearance of information theory on the psychological scene, and since the results are analyzed in terms of the concepts of information theory, I shall have to preface my discussion with a few remarks about this theory.

span.label: recoding —causes→ span of immediate memory
span.note: status: CONJECTURED at this point in the paper - the authors say they SUSPECT it; the demonstration follows · direction on the measure: increases
span.quote: Since there is a large discrepancy in the amount of information recalled in these two cases, we suspect at once that a recoding procedure could be used to increase the span of immediate memory for binary digits.

span.label: span of absolute judgment —distinct-from→ span of immediate memory
span.note: RE-GROUNDS miller1956-magical-number[0]: the old span named ONE endpoint.
span.quote: In spite of the coincidence that the magical number seven appears in both places, the span of absolute judgment and the span of immediate memory are quite different kinds of limitations that are imposed on our ability to process information.

span.label: recoding —causes→ chunk
span.quote: It is reasonably obvious that this kind of recoding increases the bits per chunk, and packages the binary sequence into a form that can be retained within the span of immediate memory.

span.label: 7 ± 2 — the limit on the span of absolute judgment and immediate memory
span.quote: I would propose to call this limit the span of absolute judgment , and I maintain that for unidimensional judgments this span is usually somewhere in the neighborhood of seven

span.label: about seven — the span of absolute judgment, in categories, for unidimensional stimuli
span.quote: I would propose to call this limit the span of absolute judgment , and I maintain that for unidimensional judgments this span is usually somewhere in the neighborhood of seven.

span.label: about seven items — the span of immediate memory, in chunks - a different quantity that happens to have the same number
span.quote: Everybody knows that there is a finite span of immediate memory and that for a lot of different kinds of test materials this span is about seven items in length.

span.label: about six objects — the span of attention, at a glance - the third of the three limits
span.quote: I have just shown you that there is a span of absolute judgment that can distinguish about seven categories and that there is a span of attention that will encompass about six objects at a glance.

span.label: at least 150 — the span of absolute judgment once many dimensions are used with crude judgments on each
span.quote: 91] more dimensions and requiring crude, binary, yes-no judgments on each attribute we can extend the span of absolute judgment from seven to at least 150.

span.label: one bit — the unit, defined as a choice between two equally likely alternatives
span.quote: One bit of information is the amount of information that we need to make a decision between two equally likely alternatives.

span.label: The span of absolute judgment (one-dimensional stimuli) and the span of immediate memory both hit a limit around seven — a channel-capacity bound on how much information an observer can transmit.
span.quote: This discontinuity at seven is, of course, suggestive. Is this the same basic process that limits our

span.quote: Perhaps there is something deep and profound behind all these sevens, something just calling out for us to discover it. But I suspect that it is only a pernicious, Pythagorean coincidence.
